one_liner: Forecasts daily parcel intake, occupancy and pickups for Pitt's residence-hall mailrooms to drive day-by-day staffing and capacity planning.
problem: Campus mailrooms get surges (move-in, Halloween, Valentine's) and Tower B's lockers overflow; ops has no forecast for staffing or for how many parcels are actually held.
target_user: Pitt Mailing Services / residence-hall mailroom operations managers.
core_loop: Raw WTS package export CSV -> data.py cleaning -> per-site model selection via rolling-origin CV (Poisson/Tweedie/BayesRidge/HGB) -> dwell survival model (Kaplan-Meier) converts intake to occupancy/pickups -> staffing.py labour hours -> weekplan.py current-week CSV for a Power BI dashboard.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Locker counts (1000 pool), headcount FTE, shift hours, handout seconds are marked PLACEHOLDER pending Operations. Power BI report and ElevenLabs spoken briefing are described in README but not in repo; elevenLabs.py is a 12-line hello-world stub not wired to the pipeline. Ruskin site unmodelled; Saturday coverage 0.54 vs 0.80 target (documented open problems).
demo_risks: No UI in repo: demo is terminal tables unless Power BI file exists locally. train takes ~40s. Data files are 11-21MB CSVs. ElevenLabs narration not implemented, so Out Loud claim would be hollow.
ui_experience: None in repo. CLI prints text tables; README specifies a Power BI dashboard (slicers, matrix, cards) to be built from outputs/week_plan.csv.
integrity_flags: PII committed: packagestats.csv/xlsx contain recipient names and searchresults(1).csv contains staff names, tracked in git despite .gitignore and a README warning that they must not be pushed. Hardcoded ElevenLabs API key committed in elevenLabs.py. First README commit 2026-09-18 (pre-hack, 3 lines). Entire 2,982-line pipeline plus 554-line README landed in a single commit at 02:48 Sept 20. Data pulled via temp admin access Sept 3-9 (disclosed in config).
ai_scaffolding_flags: No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md. README prose volume and one-shot commit shape suggest heavy LLM-assisted authoring; README states no LLM in the product itself.
novelty_notes: Uncommon problem space (campus mailroom ops research). Genuine mechanism: dwell-time survival curve converting intake to true occupancy, purge detection by parcel age, regime-stratified survival. Key insight that Tower B's problem is non-collection, not demand.
need_notes: Two years of real data (109k parcels, 9 mailrooms), an email thread with Operations, measured handling times, quantified backlog (3,596 held vs 741/day peak intake). Strong domain grounding; no end-user quotes.
wow_moment: The pivot slide: 'Tower B does not need more lockers; a 30-day return-to-sender rule cuts peak holdings ~90%' backed by real occupancy data.
score_rationale: Real operational data science with a defensible pipeline and a sharp insight, but the deliverable is a CLI producing CSVs; dashboard and voice briefing are unbuilt. No Wrapper fits on substance yet lacks a demo judges can try. PII and API key committed are serious hygiene failures.
judge_summary: A serious forecasting pipeline on two years of real Pitt mailroom data that argues Tower B's overflow is a collection-policy problem, not demand. Impressive analysis, but judges see terminal output only; no dashboard or voice feature exists in the repo, and private data plus an API key were committed.

one_liner: A Pyxel top-down zombie survival roguelite with auto-fire, level-up abilities, and a merchant van that drives around the city running over zombies.
core_loop: main.py Game.update: WASD move -> spatial-hash zombie queries -> flow-field (BFS) zombie pathfinding -> auto-target nearest zombie and fire -> pickups magnetize (XP/gold) -> level-up ability choice (8 abilities) -> shop van drives to random spot, parks, sells items -> death/restart.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Nothing mocked; F2 demo mode (3x rewards) and F4 dev grant exist for demos. No audio despite a 'Sounds' PR title (no pyxel.sound/play calls). README calls it 'asset-free' but it loads PNG sprite sheets via Pillow.
demo_risks: Low: local Python game, no network. Needs pyxel+Pillow installed; 256x144 window is tiny on a projector unless scaled. Pillow-based PNG quantization at startup could fail on a missing sheet (falls back to circles).
ui_experience: Pixel-art 256x144 procedural + sprite-sheet rendering: animated 8-direction player sheets, walk/hurt/death zombie sheets (2 enemy types), 48-frame rotating minivan, 64x64 Tiled city map with 3 layers and collisions, HUD, shop/level-up/upgrade/game-over menus, dev overlay.
integrity_flags: Committed .venv (1,117 files, ~666k lines) in the 13:02 'base program' commit despite .gitignore. Third-party sprite/tileset PNGs (All_Tilesets, minivan sheet, Demon/Blood Monster) uncredited. Work began at hack start (11:09); base program at 13:02 was ~200 lines. 51 pytest tests.
ai_scaffolding_flags: One merge commit authored by copilot-swe-agent[bot] (GitHub Copilot coding agent). Very long explanatory docstrings in shop.py/assets.py alongside dense one-line code suggest mixed AI/human authorship. No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md.
novelty_notes: Vampire Survivors clone; the distinctive twist is the merchant as a pathfinding van that drives orthogonally through the city, sweeps turn frames, backs up when stuck, and kills zombies in its path.
need_notes: No problem or user need; purely a game.
wow_moment: The shop van barrelling through a horde on its way to its next parking spot, then opening for business.
score_rationale: Complete, playable, tested game loop with real sprite animation, tilemap collisions and flow-field AI, built in 24h. Genre is very familiar and there is no problem statement, so novelty and need are low. No LLM, so No Wrapper is the only real fit, though the 'hard thing' is modest. .venv commit is a hygiene miss.
judge_summary: A finished, playable pixel-art zombie survival game with eight abilities and a merchant van that drives around the map. Fun and polished for a hackathon, but a well-worn genre with no problem it solves.

project_name: PGH Transit (Pittsburgh Regional Transit real-time bus app)
one_liner: Keyless real-time PRT bus tracker: Node proxy over PRT's public GTFS-realtime feeds plus a Leaflet web page and an Expo mobile app showing nearby stops, live buses and arrival countdowns.
problem: Riders want to see where buses actually are and when they arrive at nearby stops without a PRT developer key.
core_loop: Browser geolocation -> GET /api/stops/nearby (haversine over committed stops.txt) -> auto-fetch predictions for closest 6 stops to discover routes -> poll /api/vehicles every 15s (backend fetches and decodes PRT GTFS-RT protobuf, 10s cache) -> bus markers glide on map; tap stop -> live arrival countdown; route polylines from shapes.txt.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Web index.html is fully wired to the backend and live PRT feed. Mobile app: config.js API_BASE_URL is '10.0.5.245' with no scheme or port (axios calls would fail as committed); api.js calls /api/routes/:rt/directions and /stops endpoints that the server does not implement (unused by screens); Google Maps keys are placeholders. Static GTFS (21MB shapes.txt) committed.
demo_risks: Depends on live internet access to truetime.portauthority.org and Esri tiles; if the PRT feed is down or slow there are no buses. Backend must run locally on port 4000. Browser geolocation permission required (falls back to Pittsburgh center but then shows no nearby stops). Mobile build likely non-functional without config fix.
ui_experience: Web: styled sidebar (Oswald/Inter fonts, gold/river palette) with Stops/Routes/Stop tabs, Leaflet map, bus chips colored per route, route polylines, arrival rows with DUE state. Mobile: 3 stack screens (Map, Routes picker with search, Stop arrivals) with animated bus markers rotated by heading.
integrity_flags: Single commit at 23:38 Sept 19 containing the entire polished codebase. README and code comments are written in a tutorial/hand-off voice ('this is the keyless version', 'if you later get a BusTime API key approved'), consistent with one-shot LLM generation. backend/package.json oddly depends on expo. No team info anywhere.
ai_scaffolding_flags: No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, but style and single-commit shape strongly suggest LLM-generated code and README.
novelty_notes: Real-time transit trackers are a very common category (PRT's own app, Transit). Small twists: keyless GTFS-RT decoding, auto-tracking routes discovered from nearby-stop predictions, gliding markers.
need_notes: Plausible generic need; no evidence, quotes or differentiation from existing apps given.
wow_moment: Open the page and buses near you are already moving along real streets without picking a route.
score_rationale: The web path is wired to real live PRT data and looks decent, but the mobile app is broken as committed, the category is saturated, no track is targeted, and the one-commit LLM-shaped history offers little evidence of hackathon effort.
judge_summary: A clean live map of Pittsburgh buses using PRT's public feed. Works in the browser, but it is a familiar transit tracker with no track fit, a broken mobile config, and one late-night commit for the whole project.

one_liner: LeetCode-style site where you take a C++ snippet and submit a faster version; the server compiles it with g++, times it, and stores the submission.
problem: No README; implied: practice performance optimization of C++ code with measured runtimes.
target_user: Programmers wanting to practice low-level optimization (implied).
core_loop: Frontend select snippet -> GET /api/code/snippet/{id} fills textarea -> POST /api/code/run {snippetId, sourceCode} -> RunService writes temp_program.cc, runs g++, executes binary, Stopwatch runtime -> saves Submission row -> returns runtime/stdout/stderr, which the frontend only console.logs.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Frontend dropdown hardcodes a single 'Snippet 1' option; run result is never rendered (console.log only); no leaderboard, no correctness check of output, no comparison against baseline; DB connection string is a placeholder (fake_user/fake_password); backend.http still hits the template /weatherforecast.
demo_risks: Needs a reachable Postgres with migrations applied and g++ in the container. Fixed temp file names mean concurrent runs clobber each other. Arbitrary unsandboxed code execution on a public Cloud Run service (commit literally titled 'add unsanitized execution'); no timeouts, so an infinite loop hangs the request.
ui_experience: Unstyled: a <select>, a 10x50 textarea, and a Run button; index.css is empty; results only visible in browser devtools.
integrity_flags: No project README (only the Vite template README). Unsanitized remote code execution deployed publicly. Solo committer, 4 commits, work stopped 23:37 Sept 19.
novelty_notes: Optimization-golf platforms are a modest twist on the very familiar online-judge category; nothing distinctive is implemented beyond compile-and-time.
need_notes: No problem statement or user given.
wow_moment: None; the only visible interaction is a textarea whose result goes to the console.
score_rationale: Backend compiles, runs and persists submissions, so a slice works, but the product loop (compare, rank, display) is absent and the UI is a bare textarea that never shows results. No track fit, no README, and an unsandboxed public code runner.
judge_summary: A bare-bones backend that compiles and times user-submitted C++ and stores it in Postgres. The idea of optimization challenges is fine, but nothing is shown on screen and there is no leaderboard, README, or safety.

one_liner: Type what you feel like eating; Claude writes a budget recipe and the app prices every ingredient against a hand-verified Target grocery CSV, showing total, per-serving cost and store-brand savings.
problem: College students on tight budgets do not know what a meal will actually cost to buy before choosing a recipe.
target_user: College students cooking in dorms/small apartments (Pittsburgh Target shoppers).
stack: Python demo script (anthropic SDK + web_search tool)
core_loop: Planner.tsx input/chips -> POST /api/plan -> route.ts calls Anthropic with a JSON-only system prompt -> parses recipe ingredients -> lib/pantry.ts tokenizes, expands synonyms, scores against 1,072-item Target CSV with category hints and store-brand detection -> returns priced shopping list, total, per-serving, savings, missing -> rendered in UI.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Prices are a static CSV (Target, Pittsburgh, Sept 2026), not live; no store/location selection. pythondemo.py is a separate CLI experiment (web-search recipe lookup) not used by the web app. Layout metadata still says 'Create Next App'.
demo_risks: Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and internet; each query is a live model call (latency, possible non-JSON output handled with a 502 error state). Matching is heuristic; wrong-aisle matches possible on stage. Loading/error states exist.
ui_experience: Single page, custom CSS with clean typographic hierarchy: prompt field, example chips, price bar (total / per serving), savings line, shopping list rows with product+unit and 'Not sold at Target', numbered steps, footer with data provenance. Tidy but plain.
integrity_flags: Top-level README is empty (1 byte). Repeated commit message 'Update print statement from Hello to Goodbye' attached to unrelated changes (3x). 1,072-row 'hand-verified' price CSV uploaded 3h into the hack (data collection may predate the event). No secrets committed; key read from env.
ai_scaffolding_flags: web/CLAUDE.md -> @AGENTS.md; AGENTS.md is the block Next.js 16 'next dev' auto-generates (not evidence of agent use by itself). Commit 'Add recipe planner with Claude'.
novelty_notes: Recipe/meal planners are common; the twist is grounding the LLM recipe in a real, verified local price list with store-brand vs name-brand savings and honest 'not sold here' gaps.
need_notes: Plausible student budgeting pain; some effort evidence (hand-checked prices) but no user validation.
wow_moment: Tap 'tacos for four people' and see a real Target total and per-serving price appear with a 'saved $X buying store brand' line.
score_rationale: Works end to end with sensible error handling and a non-trivial 500-line matcher over real price data, but it is an LLM recipe wrapper in a crowded category with a static dataset, no strong track, and a plain single-screen UI.
judge_summary: Ask for a meal, get a Claude recipe priced line-by-line against 1,000 real Target prices with store-brand savings. Functional and honest about gaps, but a familiar idea with a simple one-page UI.

one_liner: A supply-chain investigation inbox that turns public disruption signals (weather alerts, company statements) into prioritized supplier/material/purchase-order exposures with clickable evidence.
problem: Purchasing managers at small manufacturers cannot quickly connect news of a flood or plant shutdown to which of their open orders are at risk, or explain why.
target_user: Purchasing manager at a small or midsize US manufacturer.
core_loop: Intended: document/NWS/RSS ingestion -> model extraction -> evidence validation -> entity match -> exposure ranking -> alert. Implemented: lib/scenario.ts hardcoded workspace (3 alerts, sources, evidence, orders) -> inbox page with URL-driven filters -> alert detail page (facts/context/inference/unknowns) -> evidence drawer with exact excerpts -> event->facility->supplier->material->order dependency path.
mocked_or_hardcoded: Everything is fixture data from scenario.ts (labelled 'Scenario data' in the UI). No ingestion, no model call, no persistence, no API routes, no investigation actions; sidebar items Supply network / Sources / Review queue are 'Soon' placeholders. Development plan marks only steps 1.1-2.3 of 8 phases complete.
demo_risks: Low technical risk (static Next.js app), but a judge asking 'upload a document' or 'where does the model run' will find nothing; Xtract's extraction/traceability criteria are only mocked. Last commit 18:08 Sept 19, so nothing after day one.
ui_experience: Polished enterprise-dashboard look: sidebar shell with brand mark, summary cards, priority/event/workflow badges, animated radar empty state, filter form, evidence drawer with focus trap and Escape handling, dependency path component, custom 404. Responsive breakpoints checked by a Playwright script.
integrity_flags: First commit (16:34 Sept 19) already contained an 822-line PRD dated that day, a 159-line phased dev plan, 1,089 lines of CSS and 459 lines of fixtures (9,560 lines total), which points to LLM-generated spec and scaffold. Single author, 4 commits, all on Sept 19. Docs (~980 lines) are roughly half the size of the code, not larger.
ai_scaffolding_flags: CLAUDE.md -> @AGENTS.md (Next.js auto-generated block). docs/FAULTLINE_PRD.md and docs/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md read as agent-oriented execution plans ('First executable task', gates per step).
novelty_notes: Supply-chain risk intelligence is an established enterprise category (Resilinc, Everstream) but rare at hackathons; the known/inferred/unknown framing and evidence-first design are thoughtful. Nothing novel is implemented beyond the UI.
need_notes: PRD gives personas and a coherent job-to-be-done but no data, quotes, or domain evidence; the need is argued, not shown.
wow_moment: Clicking a claim opens the exact quoted source excerpt, and the event->facility->supplier->material->order chain is laid out with evidence on every link.
score_rationale: Strong concept and a genuinely polished front end aimed squarely at Xtract, but the entire signal-to-insight engine is a fixture; there is no ingestion, extraction, model, or persistence, so the track's core criteria are unmet. Work ended after ~7 hours on day one.
judge_summary: A handsome mock of a supply-chain risk inbox: three fictional alerts with clickable evidence and a dependency path. The design thinking is good, but no documents are ingested and no model runs; it is a front end for a product that was never built.

one_liner: A Godot 4 3D driving game where you pilot an 'armored ambulance' through a low-poly city with a siren blaring, intended to reach patients.
core_loop: Intended: main menu DRIVE -> level -> drive ambulance to patient -> deliver. Implemented: MainMenue.tscn (DRIVE/OPTIONS/QUIT) -> Levels/level.tscn containing a 7,743-node city (buildings, roads, trees, rocks), a CharacterBody3D 'KrankenIt' with 23-line WASD slide movement + gravity, chase camera, looping music and siren AudioStreamPlayers, and a Patient marker (yellow ring with an Area3D and no script).
mocked_or_hardcoded: Menu wiring is broken: Menues.cs loads 'res://level.tscn' and 'res://scene/options.tscn' (neither exists; level is at res://Levels/level.tscn) and its Main._Ready never runs because MainMenue.tscn is the project main scene, so DRIVE adds a null node. No objective, scoring, pickup/delivery, pedestrians logic, damage, or vehicle physics (CharacterBody3D, not VehicleBody3D). Commit message: 'Patient is present, no script rn'.
demo_risks: Playable only by opening Levels/level.tscn directly in the Godot editor; 6.4MB scene with thousands of collision shapes may load slowly. Requires Godot 4.7 with .NET support. Nothing to 'win' in a 3-minute demo.
ui_experience: 3D city with textured buildings, roads, nature props, low-poly car model, directional light; custom-font main menu and pause menu themes; siren and music audio. Visual assets are mostly third-party packs.
integrity_flags: Brief called it Unity; it is Godot 4.7 C#/GDScript. Heavy use of third-party asset packs (8 car models, LandScape pack with README.txt, FabConvert zip, Nature FBX) uncredited in README. Two-line README. 292 .import files and a 6.4MB scene committed. Three committers, work through 08:25 Sept 20.
ai_scaffolding_flags: None. GDScript is the Godot CharacterBody3D template with comments intact.
novelty_notes: Ambulance driving games are a known niche; the German 'tank ambulance' joke is the only twist, and it is not realized in gameplay.
wow_moment: Siren wailing while a low-poly ambulance slides through a surprisingly large 3D city.
score_rationale: A large 3D city was assembled from asset packs with audio and menus, but the game has no objective, the car is a sliding CharacterBody3D with template movement, and the menu-to-level wiring is broken as committed. Nominal No Wrapper fit only.
judge_summary: A 3D city you can slide an ambulance around with a siren playing. Looks like a game from a distance, but there is no patient delivery, no scoring, and the main menu cannot actually launch the level.
